name: Beef Cuts
summary: Which beef cuts are tender and which are tough, and how to cook each one.

sections.heading: Tender vs. tough
blocks: Where a cut comes from decides how to cook it. Muscles along the back (the rib and loin) barely work, so they're tender and best cooked fast and hot, to the doneness you like. Hard-working muscles (shoulder, chest, legs) are full of connective tissue: tough when cooked fast, wonderfully tender when cooked low and slow until they fall apart.
Steaks are labeled with US names below; other names include common UK and restaurant names.

rows: Lots of marbling, rich flavor. Forgiving.
New York strip, Kansas City strip, sirloin (UK)
Leaner than ribeye with a good chew and beefy flavor.
Mild and lean; expensive. Don't cook past medium.
A strip and a piece of tenderloin on one bone; the tenderloin side cooks faster.

Marinate; cook no more than medium; slice thinly against the grain.
Thin and fast-cooking; slice against the grain.
From the shoulder but tender; great value.

blocks.text: **Slice against the grain**: look for the lines running through the meat and cut across them. It shortens the fibers, so even chewy cuts like flank and skirt eat tender.

sections.heading: Braising cuts
blocks: These are the cheap, flavorful cuts. Cook them low and slow with liquid until fork-tender: see [Braising & Stewing](guide:braising-and-stewing).

rows: The all-purpose braising cut; buy a roast and cube it yourself.
The flat is leaner, the point is fattier.
Rich and meaty; brown them well first.
The marrow in the bone enriches the liquid.
Lots of gelatin; slow but worth it.

sections.heading: Ground beef
blocks: Ground beef is labeled by how lean it is. **80/20** (80% lean, 20% fat, often from chuck) makes the juiciest burgers and meatballs. **85/15** and **90/10** suit tacos, sauces and chili, where you'd pour off extra fat anyway. Leaner beef dries out in burgers.

blocks.text: Grinding spreads surface bacteria through the meat, so cook ground beef to 160°F (71°C), even in burgers you'd like pink. See the [doneness chart](guide:doneness-and-food-safety#doneness-chart).

sections.heading: Grades
blocks: USDA grades beef mostly by marbling, the flecks of fat in the meat that keep it juicy:

items: **Prime**: the most marbling; mostly sold to restaurants and at butchers.
**Choice**: the everyday supermarket grade, with good marbling.
**Select**: leaner and less forgiving; best braised or marinated.

blocks: Grade matters most for steaks and roasts cooked quickly; for braising cuts, Choice or Select is fine.
